stories.headline: UAE says FlyDubai co-pilot attacked captain with cockpit axe
stories.dek: Officials say the co-pilot tried to seize the plane on a Tel Aviv flight before passengers and crew helped stop him.
paragraphs: The UAE says a FlyDubai co-pilot attacked the captain with a cockpit crash axe on Wednesday and tried to take control of a flight bound for Tel Aviv. Prosecutors called it a terrorist act on Saturday as investigators examined physical and digital evidence and regional airlines suspended some Israel routes.

The flight was carrying 182 people. The injured captain, Indian pilot Smit Machchhar, said he opened the cockpit door while under attack, letting crew and passengers rush in and subdue the co-pilot. Reports identify the co-pilot as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, who had earlier been removed from flying in Oman.

Investigators still need to establish the co-pilot's motive, his contacts, and how he passed hiring and security checks to work for FlyDubai. It is also unclear how rules meant to restrict some foreign pilots on Israel-bound flights were applied. The UAE and Israel are arranging repatriation flights for stranded passengers.
stories.changes: Passengers on some UAE-Israel routes now face cancellations, rerouting, and tighter scrutiny of cockpit and crew vetting.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean commercial flying in the region has broadly become unsafe or that every disruption points to a wider plot.

cover.title: UAE says FlyDubai co-pilot attacked captain on Tel Aviv flight
cover.standfirst: UAE prosecutors said a FlyDubai co-pilot used a cockpit crash axe to attack the captain and tried to seize a flight carrying 182 people to Tel Aviv on Wednesday. The wounded captain opened the cockpit door, allowing crew and passengers to stop the attack, while investigators examine motive, vetting and security failures.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat acid-green ground, show only a black cutout of the cockpit doorway seen from the cabin, slightly off-centre high in frame, with a dense wedge of black arms and shoulders surging into it from both sides as if passengers and crew have just piled forward to stop someone inside. Keep the lower third almost empty for type. The white void inside the doorway must cleanly resolve into the unmistakable silhouette of Israel, so the fight at the cockpit door and the Tel Aviv destination land in the same glance.
art.note: Sharp, tense collage in dark blue, grey and emergency red.
art.second_beat: First you see a cockpit struggle in progress; a beat later the empty shape inside the doorway turns into Israel, tying the attempted seizure specifically to the Tel Aviv flight.

stories.headline: Russian strike damages Kyiv bridge and halts traffic again
stories.dek: The hit tore up the road surface and trolleybus wires on Kyiv’s Northern Bridge, with no casualties reported.
paragraphs: A Russian strike early Saturday damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge, closing it to traffic for a third day of disruption in the capital. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said the blast wrecked part of the road surface and trolleybus cables. Russia said it targeted the bridge because Ukraine uses it for military transport.

Kyiv has six road bridges over the Dnipro River, which splits the city. On Friday, Russian attacks had already forced the full or partial closure of three of them. Russia has recently widened its targets beyond the front, hitting apartment blocks, warehouses, gas stations and data centers as air attacks on cities intensify.

It is not clear how long repairs will take or whether more bridge strikes will follow. There were no reported deaths or injuries, but the attacks are testing daily movement across the capital. The wider war remains stuck, with no clear sign of a peace deal and both sides still trading long-range strikes.
stories.changes: For people in Kyiv, crossing the river may take longer and daily travel can be disrupted even far from the front line.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Kyiv has been cut in two or that Russia has made a major battlefield breakthrough.

cover.title: Russia damages a Kyiv bridge and halts city traffic
cover.standfirst: A Russian strike hit Kyiv’s Northern Bridge early Saturday, damaging the road and trolleybus wires and stopping traffic. The attack came after other bridge closures a day earlier, leaving movement across the Dnipro River harder as Russia presses a campaign to disrupt daily life in the capital.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Show Kyiv’s Northern Bridge in one stark side elevation, split horizontally into two misaligned states of the same moment. In the upper band, the span is intact and a single unmistakable Kyiv trolleybus is moving across under taut wires; in the lower band, the same bus is stopped dead at a fresh gouge torn out of the roadway, with the trolley poles still reaching up toward wires that have vanished and a few snapped cables hanging loose. Keep it to black and deep blue with one hard red accent only inside the ripped road wound; leave the lower third largely open as dark river for type.
art.note: Cold, stark, restrained palette with river blue, concrete gray and a violent black scar.
art.second_beat: First you read a simple before/after bridge image; then you notice the trolleybus poles still straining toward missing wires, which turns damage into the precise fact of traffic being halted.

stories.headline: Russian strike damages Kyiv’s Northern Bridge after South Bridge attacks
stories.dek: The hit tore up road surface and trolleybus wires on one of Kyiv’s busiest Dnipro crossings, adding to days of bridge closures and traffic jams.
paragraphs: Russian forces struck Kyiv’s Northern Bridge on the morning of October 3, damaging the road surface and overhead trolleybus power lines. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said traffic was partly restricted. The attack came after two days of strikes on the city’s Southern Bridge, widening pressure on Kyiv’s main river crossings.

Kyiv has nine bridges across the Dnipro River for road, rail, and pedestrian traffic. The Northern and Southern bridges are among the city’s busiest routes. Strikes on the Southern Bridge on October 1 and 2 damaged a support, guardrail, road surface, and a concrete barrier protecting the metro line.

It is still unclear how badly the Northern Bridge was damaged, how long restrictions will last, and whether more crossings will be targeted. The recent attacks were reported as the first wartime strikes on Kyiv’s Dnipro bridges. Other bridges have already seen partial closures as traffic was redirected across the city.
stories.changes: Crossing Kyiv east to west may take longer now, with fewer open routes across the Dnipro and heavier traffic on the bridges still operating.
stories.unchanged: Kyiv still has multiple Dnipro crossings, so the city is not cut in two and transport has not stopped completely.

cover.title: Russian strikes damage a second major bridge in Kyiv
cover.standfirst: Russian forces hit Kyiv’s Northern Bridge on October 3, damaging the road and trolleybus power lines and forcing a partial closure. The strike followed at least three drone attacks over two days on the Southern Bridge, one of the capital’s other key crossings over the Dnipro.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Show the Northern Bridge approach in three-quarter view, cropped tight so the boxy Kyiv trolleybus is unmistakable: twin poles sprung loose and flung upward, no longer touching the overhead wires, the bus skewed diagonally across the lane at the very lip of a torn, gouged patch of roadway. Behind it, compress a dense wedge of halted car roofs into a black traffic jam, while one broken catenary line sags sharply across the upper half like a snapped cable; keep the lower third largely open asphalt for type. Strip out any blast, smoke or skyline—the image is only the city’s transport system abruptly severed mid-commute.
art.note: Severe and spare; cold gray-blue palette with one harsh burn-black accent.
art.second_beat: First you see a stranded trolleybus and jam; a beat later you realise the whole crossing has been ‘unplugged’ because the bridge’s own wiring and road surface have both failed.

stories.headline: Car hits Newcastle Knights supporters gathered near match crowds
stories.dek: Supporters rushed to help the injured and held the alleged driver after a car went into people in Newcastle.
paragraphs: A car hit a crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters in Newcastle, injuring people gathered around the team’s fan traffic. The incident was reported two hours ago. Fans nearby became first responders, giving aid to the injured and detaining the alleged driver until authorities could take over.

The Newcastle Knights are a National Rugby League club with a large local following, so match areas can fill quickly before and after games. In Australia, crowd safety plans usually focus on barriers, traffic control and police presence, but vehicles near pedestrians remain a serious risk when streets are busy.

Officials have not yet said how many people were hurt, how severe the injuries are, or why the driver entered the crowd. It is also unclear exactly where the crash happened and what security measures were in place at the time. Police inquiries are likely to focus on motive and access.
stories.changes: People heading to big sporting events may see tighter vehicle barriers and more controlled pedestrian zones.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean every stadium crowd is unsafe or that fans should avoid public events altogether.

cover.title: Car hits Newcastle Knights supporters gathered near match crowd
cover.standfirst: A car drove into Newcastle Knights supporters in Newcastle, leaving fans to treat the injured and hold the alleged driver. Authorities have not yet said how many people were hurt or why the vehicle entered the crowd. Police are now investigating the scene and the event security setup.

art.label: Flat character
art.concept: Seen from above, compress the scene into a dense stream of Newcastle Knights supporters moving toward the stadium: repeated dark-blue shirt blocks with the unmistakable red chevron across many backs, all flowing in one direction. Cut one small clay-coloured car diagonally through that pattern so it creates a sharp torn gap rather than a crash tableau; at the break, a few simplified supporters pivot inward, with two kneeling at the edge of the gap and a tight cluster closing around the stopped car. Keep the lower third mostly open off-white, with the crowd band and rupture riding across the middle.
art.note: Calm, serious mood; muted evening colours with small sharp reds and blues.
art.second_beat: First read: a car has violently broken the fan crowd pattern; second beat: the crowd doesn’t just scatter, it turns inward to help the injured and restrain the driver.

stories.headline: Victoria cut mental health watchdog powers staff and budget
stories.dek: Leaked documents show the commission lost independence, data access and half its resources after being created to police mental health reform.
paragraphs: Leaked internal documents show Victoria’s government sharply reduced the powers, budget and staff of its mental health watchdog. The report matters now because a new single commissioner has just started, inheriting a body that insiders say can no longer properly monitor services or track promised reforms.

The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission was set up after Victoria’s royal commission into mental health. It was meant to independently oversee the system and hold government to account. The documents say the Department of Health withheld important data, while legislation later replaced four commissioners with one.

It is still unclear why the government made the changes so quickly and how much oversight the commission can now exercise in practice. Key questions remain about emergency wait times, use of restraints, youth bed shortages, discharges into homelessness and whether mental health funds are being diverted elsewhere.
stories.changes: Victorians may now have a weaker independent body checking whether mental health services are safe, funded and improving as promised.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean mental health services have stopped, or that every hospital or program has failed.

cover.title: Victoria weakened its mental health watchdog after royal commission
cover.standfirst: Leaked documents say Victoria cut the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission’s powers, staff and budget, then replaced four commissioners with one. The body was created to oversee reform after the royal commission. A new commissioner has now taken over with fewer tools and less independence.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat acid-green ground, show a black government guard dog in stark cutout silhouette being vacuum-sealed inside a clear crinkling specimen bag mid-suction: the plastic is collapsing hard around its muzzle, ribs and paws, forcing the body into an awkward compressed shape while the dog still strains forward, glaring out. Keep it brutally simple — no hand, no labels, no extra props — just the bag’s circular suction point, the wrinkled plastic tension, and the hound’s spiked collar and watchdog stance made unmistakable; leave the lower third mostly open and quiet for type.
art.note: Sharp, accusatory collage in muted greys with harsh red accents.
art.second_beat: First read: a watchdog is being physically neutralised; second beat: the body doing the sealing is the same system the dog was created to police.

stories.headline: G7 plans 100 million barrel oil and diesel release
stories.dek: The group aims to add fuel to the market after war-driven price rises pushed up petrol and diesel costs.
paragraphs: G7 countries plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from reserves as fuel prices keep rising during the war in Ukraine. The goal is to put more supply into the market now, in the hope that extra barrels will ease pressure on drivers, businesses and heating costs.

The G7 is a group of large rich economies that often coordinate on trade, sanctions and energy. Oil and diesel prices have climbed for months as the war disrupted supply and markets reacted to uncertainty. Higher fuel costs feed into transport, food and other daily expenses in the US and many other countries.

It is still unclear how quickly the fuel will reach buyers, how the barrels will be split among countries, and how long any price relief will last. Reserve releases can soften a shortage for a time, but they do not fix the war, refinery limits or wider problems in global energy supply.

cover.title: G7 plans 100 million barrel oil and diesel release
cover.standfirst: The group aims to add fuel to the market after war-driven price rises pushed up petrol and diesel costs.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On warm light-grey seamless paper, place a single black petrol nozzle diagonally so it has just been dropped or pulled away, with a dark fuel spill emerging from its tip. Closest to the nozzle the spill is still liquid, but as it runs across the frame it resolves into exactly 100 tiny, unmistakable oil-barrel-shaped droplets spreading outward; keep the lower third largely clear, with the action sitting higher and to one side so type can sit cleanly over open ground.
art.second_beat: First you see a fuel spill; a beat later you realise the spill is turning into countable released barrels, converting strategic reserves into pump fuel while hinting that 100 million barrels may still disperse fast.

stories.headline: Trump expected to give Jay Clayton a new AI role
stories.dek: Reports say Clayton could oversee AI policy and industry conduct alongside his current intelligence post.
paragraphs: Donald Trump is expected to appoint Jay Clayton as a new White House AI czar, according to reports cited by crypto news outlets. The role would add AI innovation and development to Clayton’s work as US intelligence chief. The reported plan comes as the administration pushes to shape fast-growing AI systems.

An AI czar is usually a senior official who coordinates policy across agencies and acts as a main contact for industry. The summary says Clayton may also oversee a form of self-policing by technology chief executives. That suggests the White House wants companies to set some standards while the government keeps a central hand on strategy.

The reports do not say when the appointment would be announced, what legal powers the job would carry, or how it would fit with existing agencies. It is also unclear which companies would be involved, what self-policing would mean in practice, and how conflicts between national security and AI growth would be handled.
stories.changes: If confirmed, one senior official could become a main gatekeeper for how the US government deals with AI companies.
stories.unchanged: This does not by itself create new AI laws or immediately change the tools people use at work or at home.

cover.title: Trump is expected to put Jay Clayton in charge of AI
cover.standfirst: Reports say Donald Trump plans to give US intelligence chief Jay Clayton a second job overseeing artificial intelligence policy. The role would cover AI development and industry self-policing by technology executives. No formal announcement, powers or start date have been made public.

art.label: Minimal mark
art.concept: Show a single tall White House window, placed slightly off-centre in a wide white field. The upper half remains a crisp, recognisable sash window; the lower half has seamlessly transformed into the dark circular lens and housing of a surveillance camera, as if the architecture itself has changed job mid-form. Keep it flat, geometric and still, with the lower third left largely empty for type.
art.note: Firm, public-institution mood; limited red, blue and black palette.
art.second_beat: First you see the White House; a beat later you realise one office has quietly turned from government post into watching machine — intelligence authority becoming AI oversight.

stories.headline: Google launches test satellite for space-based AI data centers
stories.dek: A refrigerator-size craft carries four custom chips that will run short Gemini tasks in orbit and then shut down to cool.
paragraphs: Google has launched an experimental satellite to test whether computer hardware can run in orbit as part of a future space data center. The satellite went up on October 1 aboard a SpaceX rocket. Google says the test matters now because AI systems need more power and more computing capacity.

The craft was built with Planet and carries four tensor processing units, or TPUs. Each chip has about the computing power of one data-center server. They will run for 15 minutes at a time, handling short Gemini AI queries, then stop so the system can cool in space.

The big unknown is whether this can scale beyond a small test. Chips in space must survive heat, radiation and debris, and cooling is harder without fans or large water systems. Google plans two more launches next year, but full orbital data centers remain a distant idea.
stories.changes: It points to a future where some AI computing could happen off Earth instead of in power-hungry buildings near towns and power grids.
stories.unchanged: Your searches and chatbot requests are not suddenly running in space today, and this test does not solve AI's energy use on its own.

cover.title: Google launches a satellite to test AI computing in space
cover.standfirst: Google sent a refrigerator-size satellite into low-Earth orbit on October 1 with four custom AI chips aboard. The chips will run Gemini tasks for 15 minutes at a time, then shut down to cool. The company plans more test launches next year as it studies whether space can host future data centers.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: On a plain tabletop with a clean, quiet lower third, stage a tight grid of small handmade server racks built from simple card-and-felt modules across the upper half of the cover. One unit has just broken out of the grid and is lifting diagonally upward on a tiny pipe-cleaner rocket plume; as it rises, it is no longer a rack but a refrigerator-size satellite with a clear cutaway side showing exactly four bright chip tiles inside, plus a few small orange heat marks venting off it. Keep everything else stripped back: no stars, no extra props, just the single server becoming the orbital test craft.
art.note: Clean, technical, slightly austere; deep black, solar yellow, cold blue.
art.second_beat: First read: one machine is launching; second beat: this satellite is literally a single data-center server pulled out of the rack and tested in orbit.

stories.headline: Tennessee halts executions after inmate survives a second failed attempt
stories.dek: Lawyers say Christa Pike is unconscious on a ventilator after a botched execution, and the governor paused all executions for the rest of 2026.
paragraphs: Tennessee has halted executions for the rest of 2026 after a second failed execution this year. Lawyers for death row prisoner Christa Pike say she survived the attempt and is now unconscious on a ventilator. The pause came after the latest failure raised immediate questions about the state's execution process.

Pike is a Tennessee death row inmate. The state had already faced one botched execution earlier this year, so this case deepened concern about whether prison staff, drugs, or procedures were safe and lawful. Governors can stop scheduled executions while a state reviews how its death penalty system is being carried out.

It is still unclear what exactly went wrong during Pike's execution attempt, how serious her condition is, and whether she will recover. The state has not yet answered the central questions about responsibility, possible investigations, or whether executions will resume in 2027 after the governor's pause ends.
stories.changes: If you live in Tennessee, no further executions are expected this year while the state reviews what went wrong.
stories.unchanged: This does not end Tennessee's death penalty or erase existing death sentences.

cover.title: Tennessee pauses executions after Christa Pike survives failed attempt
cover.standfirst: Tennessee stopped all executions for the rest of 2026 after lawyers said death row prisoner Christa Pike survived a botched execution and was left unconscious on a ventilator. It was the state's second failed execution this year. Officials now face pressure to explain what happened and review the system.

art.label: Decorative flat
art.concept: Fill the cover with a dense, flat lattice of unmistakable prison bars, repeated edge to edge like a screenprinted pattern. At the center, one opening has been violently cut to the exact silhouette of an execution gurney; the severed bars bend outward mid-swing, and behind the gap is only a blank hospital-blue void with a tiny ventilator-bed silhouette far back in the emptiness. Keep the lower third quiet by letting the bar pattern continue there with no extra incident; all the force is in the missing gurney-shaped breach and the cold medical absence behind it.
art.note: Severe, restrained mood; muted red, slate gray, and off-white.
art.second_beat: First you see a prison pattern broken open; a beat later you realize the hole is the precise shape of the execution table that should be there, replaced by hospital aftermath.

stories.headline: US job growth slowed sharply in September as unemployment ticked up
stories.dek: Payrolls rose by 29,000, far below forecasts, while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2% and wage growth cooled.
paragraphs: The United States added 29,000 jobs in September, much less than expected, and the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%. The Labor Department released the figures as investors and the Federal Reserve watch for signs that higher interest rates are slowing hiring, pay growth and demand across the economy.

The report also revised earlier months lower. August job growth was cut to 133,000, and July changed from a gain to a loss of 10,000 jobs. Pay growth slowed to 3% from a year earlier. Healthcare, construction and manufacturing added jobs, while government, temp work, information and finance lost them.

The main question now is whether this is a brief weak month or the start of a broader slowdown. Other parts of the report were steadier: household employment rose, labor force participation increased, and a broader unemployment measure fell. The Fed still faces sticky inflation, so one soft payroll report may not settle its next move.
stories.changes: Borrowing costs may stop rising for now if the Fed sees weaker hiring as a sign the economy is cooling.
stories.unchanged: Most people who have jobs still have them, and one weak month does not mean the labor market has collapsed.

cover.title: US employers added only 29,000 jobs in September
cover.standfirst: The Labor Department said payrolls grew far less than expected and the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%. Earlier job counts were revised down, wage growth slowed, and investors now see the Federal Reserve as more likely to leave interest rates unchanged at its October meeting.

art.label: Maximalist doodle
art.concept: An official-looking payroll report sheet sits clipped to a plain bureau clipboard on a desk, drawn in dense maximalist doodle but staged simply enough to read instantly. Across the page, the earlier monthly bars are literal industrial columns—solid stacks made from steel beams, scaffolding, smokestacks and pay-envelope bricks—but the final September bar is only a short, unstable pile of a few pay envelopes and small work objects, actively giving way as envelopes slide off and tumble across the desk; behind it, the previous two bars are visibly pared down, with shaved-off fragments and eraser crumbs scattered nearby to imply downward revisions. Keep the lower third quiet for type by letting the fallen pieces collect mostly to one side and leaving clean desk space across the bottom.
art.note: Calm, sober mood; muted blue, gray and off-white palette.
art.second_beat: First you see a jobs chart turned physical; a beat later you notice the last bar is collapsing in real time and the earlier bars have already been cut back.
